extracted.intended_audience: OSHA rulemaking stakeholders: regulated employers, economists, state regulators, small business representatives, and public commenters on the NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological choices OSHA uses to estimate compliance costs, baseline non-compliance, and temperature exposure for the proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard; intended to inform public comment and economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount rate and annualization period
rubrics_metrics.description: All costs were annualized using a discount rate of 2 percent, consistent with OMB Circular A-4. A 10-year period is used to annualize one-time costs or other costs that do not occur every year; benefits are also annualized over a 10-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time horizon of the complete analysis is 10 years; employment and production are implicitly held constant over this horizon. Annualize one-time costs and benefits over 10 years using 2% discounting per OMB A-4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline and treatment of non-compliant entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated costs are measured against the baseline activities of the affected industries. Compliance costs are estimated only for 'non-compliant' entities with practices that currently do not conform to the proposed standard and who would therefore incur costs to comply with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define baseline to include existing conformity with proposed provisions; focus cost estimates on incremental costs for non-compliant entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline non-compliance rates methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA developed baseline non-compliance rates based on a review of existing State requirements (e.g., State heat standards, non-heat-specific paid rest break State laws), State-level workforce characteristics (e.g., prevalence of piece-rate pay, collective bargaining), other industry practices, datasets/reports, SBAR Panel feedback, and OSHA staff expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize use of State-specific data where available; use national data sources when State-specific data are absent; where no data exist, assume default non-compliance rates (sometimes distinguishing core vs non-core industries). OSHA solicits comment and alternative data/methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core vs. non-core industry differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain provisions (e.g., heat hazard evaluation and acclimatization), OSHA believes non-compliance rates among core industries may be lower than among non-core industries because core industries have more affected employees and more heat-related hazards and thus may already have policies and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating non-compliance, allow for lower default non-compliance in core industries relative to non-core industries for some provisions; but for provisions affected by broader factors (e.g., drinking water, rest break policies), assume default non-compliance rates are the same across core/non-core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of existing State heat standards and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA accounts for States that already have heat standards; employers in such States will likely have lower compliance costs since they already do some of what OSHA would require. Table VIII.C.1 shows States with existing standards and covered industries/work settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect reduced incremental costs for establishments in States with applicable heat rules; when State rules cover only subsets of NAICS codes, map 6-digit coverage to 4-digit NAICS with proportional assumptions (example: CA coverage of certain 6-digit industries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption about employers with existing HIIPPs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since all affected establishments would need to incur some cost to develop a HIIPP that meets OSHA's requirements, OSHA assumes that even establishments with existing HIIPPs would incur costs to review and modify their HIIPP to meet OSHA's requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume development/modify costs apply to all employers; OSHA provides estimated percentages for establishments with existing HIIPPs by sector/state (see Table VIII.C.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific numeric default non-compliance estimates by provision
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA provides provision-level non-compliance estimates (Table VIII.C.4) for many requirements (e.g., Develop or Modify HIIPP: 100% national; Review HIIPP: 50%; Employee Involvement: 75%; Environmental Monitoring—Outdoor/Indoor: varied by sector/state; Acclimatization, Training, Recordkeeping, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table values as preliminary defaults; OSHA distinguishes 0% compliance in some States with standards (CA, CO, MN, OR, WA) and assigns different default rates for 'Sectors 23 and 31-33', 'All Other Core Industries', and 'All Other Non-Core Industries' (often 16.7/50/90% or similar). OSHA requests feedback on these estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest break non-compliance estimation approach (initial and high triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: State-level non-compliance rate for initial heat trigger rest breaks is assumed equal to the percentage of non-union piece-rate workers in that State. High heat trigger rest break non-compliance is calculated using State paid rest break laws, State heat standards, prevalence of rest breaks in collective bargaining agreements, and union share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: non-union piece-rate employees assumed least protected; OSHA assumes nationwide that all non-piece-rate workers and union-affiliated workers are already allowed if-needed rest breaks. Solicit feedback and alternative data sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of territories and Alaska in rest-break calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest break non-compliance rates for U.S. territories were imputed using the employment-weighted average of the non-compliance rates of the States without any paid break law. Alaska's weather data did not show meeting the high trigger, but OSHA applied the same assumptions to derive a non-compliance rate that would apply if exposure met triggers; current cost for high heat trigger rest breaks is zero for Alaska.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imputation by employment-weighted averages for territories; apply Alaska assumptions cautiously and only apply high-trigger cost if methodology later finds exposure at/above trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NOAA Local Climatological Data for temperature exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used NOAA Local Climatological Data (LCD) for 2020–2022 (hourly heat index measurements) from an analyzed subset of 238 weather stations to calculate the number of workday hours meeting or exceeding heat triggers by shift type; averages across stations in each State were taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude stations with >=10% missing measurements across the three years; for each station determine workday hours meeting triggers per shift type and then average across stations within the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of outdoor data as proxy for indoor exposure without climate control
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used outdoor weather data as a proxy for high heat conditions in indoor settings without adequate climate control, acknowledging that this may overstate or understate indoor heat exposure depending on building characteristics and process heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations and uncertainty; welcome data to improve indoor exposure estimation (insulation, ventilation, process heat effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of low-humidity States for dehumidification cost assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA evaluated temperature data to identify States with relatively low levels of humidity (Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, and Utah) to inform costs related to dehumidification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust dehumidification cost assumptions for identified low-humidity States; document and request comments on humidity-related assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that employers do not make fixed investments to reduce marginal per-employee costs
rubrics_metrics.description: While some employers may be able to make fixed investments (e.g., on-site freezers, air conditioning) to reduce their marginal per-employee costs, for the purposes of this cost analysis OSHA assumes that employers do not make these adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this assumption may overestimate costs for some firms; OSHA did not explore all potential societal costs; solicits comment on other impacts and possible fixed-investment adjustments employers might adopt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost savings (reduced pacing) from rest breaks included
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA considers potential cost savings from requiring if-needed or scheduled rest breaks because evidence indicates employees pace themselves when not allowed breaks; when offered breaks, employees work more efficiently reducing employer costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimated minutes of work time lost due to pacing at initial/high heat triggers using empirical studies, translated reductions in pacing into equivalent minutes of work time saved as a share of rest break time, and monetized these savings to offset wage cost of rest breaks in unit cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and stakeholder inputs prioritized and solicited
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA used datasets/reports, SBAR Panel feedback, collective bargaining agreement reviews, and professional expertise; the agency welcomes comment on all assumptions and estimates, alternative sources, existing employer practices, and methodological changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sources and rationale; invite submission of state-level or industry-level data to refine non-compliance, exposure, and cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data exclusion and quality criteria for weather stations
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA excluded seven of the 245 stations because 10 percent or more of all heat index measurements across all three years were missing; ultimately 238 stations were analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a data completeness threshold (<=10% missing) for inclusion; document excluded stations and reasons.
